identity.name: The Advocate
identity.tag: No seat. No vote. Everything else.
identity.desc: You lead the campaign for tax fairness — the coalition outside the building, the argument inside it. Members carry the bills; you make them impossible to ignore.

intel._note: The weekly intel report. Each FACET is gated by the skill that would really buy it: Talk Story prices the chairs (live scheduling odds — rumor below `band`, honest band at `band`, exact odds + disposition at `exact` — folded in from the retired Whip Count skill 2026-08-14, since reading a chair's real disposition was always the same read as reading a coalition partner's), Procedure reads the clock (deadline warnings before they are one week out), Policy Brain puts the MEASURED hearing rate in print (it is always in the bill tooltip, but tooltips don't exist on touch). Rumor-tier odds are seeded per week+bill and may be off by one band — wrong on purpose; do not 'fix' the noise.

poles._note: Display grouping for the skill sheet — Disco groups skills under their parent attribute and colors them by it; ours group under the campaign function they serve. Order here is the order they render, and each pole's color lives in CSS as .p-<id>.

_skillsNote: skills.*.pole is WONK (inside/institutional), ORGANIZER (outside/movement) or BRIDGE (works both faces). As of 2026-08-14: Policy Brain + Procedure + Educator are wonk (3); Talk Story + Mobilizing + Base Building are organizer (3); BRIDGE IS NOW EMPTY (0) — Whip Count was retired and its chair-odds gate (`intel.odds.skill`) folded into Talk Story at the SAME thresholds (band=3/exact=5), since Whip Count's own description ('who's really with you, in the building and in the coalition') was always the same read as Talk Story's ('reading a person — a skeptical chair or a coalition partner, same skill either way'). `poles.bridge` is left defined but unused rather than deleted — renderHub already skips empty poles (`if (!ks.length) continue`), so the Bridge column simply doesn't render; a future skill can reclaim the pole without needing this note rewritten. Rhetoric was cut the same way one round earlier, into Talk Story's organizer slot — this is the same move applied to Whip Count's bridge slot, so Talk Story now single-handedly carries BOTH of Bridge's old jobs. MOBILIZING vs BASE BUILDING is the McAlevey distinction and the split is load-bearing, not flavor: mobilizing activates the already-convinced (spiky, breadth — it scales the rally), base building grows the coalition and develops leaders (slow, durability — it carries the conference hold-firm roll and the Grange on-the-record dare). Do not re-merge them into one 'organizing' stat; the whole teaching point is that turnout and durability are bought separately. NOTE: this note lives OUTSIDE the skills object on purpose — main.js does `Object.keys(data.skills)` to enumerate skill records, so a stray key INSIDE skills breaks every skill-grid render (learned the hard way, 2026-08-13).

fiscal.name: Policy Brain
fiscal.desc: Revenue estimates, fiscal notes, and whether the number on the page is real.

procedure.name: Procedure
procedure.desc: Referrals, deadlines, decking — what the rules quietly allow.

educator.name: Educator
educator.desc: Breaking a policy down until a legislator — or a brand-new advocate — actually gets it.

talkstory.name: Talk Story
talkstory.desc: Reading a person, and knowing who's really with you — a skeptical chair or a coalition partner, same skill either way.

mobilizing.name: Mobilizing
mobilizing.desc: Turning out the people already with you — how many bodies in the room, and how fast.

basebuilding.name: Base Building
basebuilding.desc: Growing the coalition and developing new leaders — whether anyone is still with you in week 14.

characters._note: Only external actors get names — people the player negotiates or contends with. The player's OWN campaign (staff, coalition) is deliberately faceless: narrative injections speak for it (dialogue node `speaker` omitted/null renders as unattributed prose via saidHtml's narration path), and its two 'Talk story' slots (`office`, `coalition`) point at a place/activity, not a person.
characters._cardNote: A character with a `card` gets a Disco-style PORTRAIT RAIL attached to the left of the dialogue window, or a compact plate on a narrow screen (charCardHtml in main.js). IT APPEARS ON THE NODE WHERE THEY FIRST SPEAK, NOT WHEN THE DIALOGUE OPENS: a scene that starts on narration (w2-kawaguchi's breezeway wait) runs full-width with no portrait, and the beats from before they arrived stay full-width above the rail. So a `speaker` key is a statement that the character is IN THE ROOM — leave it off for scene-setting, or you put them on screen early. `art` names a drawing in the PORTRAIT map — DRAWN portraits are FACELESS, the same house rule as the skill glyphs: a silhouette at a committee desk, never features. `photo` overrides it with a crop of the character's own banner photograph (site/assets/portraits/<id>.png, built by tools/make_portrait_art.py; recipe in data/raw/events/BANNERS.md) — for a character who already appears photographically in a banner, a drawn silhouette in the rail beside it was two different people. Keep the `art` key as the fallback when you add a `photo`. `tags` are short reads on how they operate; `note` is one sentence on what they control. The QUOTE is deliberately NOT stored here — it is pulled live from chairs.json `voice` via the chair whose `char` points back at this id, so a chair's own words can never drift between the two files. Only characters the player actually negotiates with need a card.

card.title: Chair, House Finance
tags: Counts votes before he spends one
card.note: Every bill carrying a dollar figure crosses his desk, and he alone decides which are heard at all. Not an opponent — a scheduler who will not spend a slot on a measure he expects to die later.

characters._souzaNote: Sen. Chris Souza is named in chairs.json (s-wam) and is the ONLY named character with no talk slot and no scene of his own. That is the point of w3-souza: House money you can walk up to, Senate money you cannot. He never speaks on screen — his scheduler, his committee members and a closed door speak for him. Do not add him to talkDefaults; a weekly 'talk to Souza' option would delete the whole premise.
characters._introducersNote: rep-x / sen-x are YOUR TWO INTRODUCERS — the members who carry the package, since the player has no seat. They are the only named characters on the player's OWN side; the faceless-campaign rule (2026-08-14) covers staff and coalition, not legislators, because a bill has a member's name on it in the real world and pretending otherwise would teach the wrong thing. NAMES ARE PLACEHOLDERS. Their gameplay record (rapport, chamber, odds terms) lives in chairs.json `introducers`, linked by `char`, exactly the way chairs are.

rally.name: Hold a rally
rally.desc: Pack the rotunda. Sign-waving, testimony trainings, kūpuna in matching shirts.

scale._note: Mobilizing turns the SAME rally into a bigger, cheaper one — more support per point of skill, less political cost. Reuses the identical skill/per math as check mods (modOf), just applied to an action's effects instead of a roll.

rally.result: The rotunda echoes for an hour. A senator's aide films it from the balcony, expressionless. Coverage runs at six and ten.

voices.text: THIS is the building's real acoustics test. Let them hear who the budget is for.
Loud once is a headline. Ask who's still texting the group chat in March.

bench.name: Build the bench
bench.desc: House meeting, then another. The people testifying in April are the ones you train in February.
bench._note: The deliberately UNGLAMOROUS action. It hands back the smallest immediate number of any move — that is the teaching, not a balance bug. Base Building's payoff is not the support tick, it is the conference hold-firm roll and the Grange on-the-record dare in the endgame. A player who only ever rallies arrives at conference with nothing left to hold the line with. Do not 'fix' this by raising the support effect to match the rally.
bench.result: Eleven people in a living room in Kalihi, folding chairs, one whiteboard. Three of them will testify for the first time next month. None of it makes the news.

voices.text: This is the only line item that compounds. Everything else you do this session, you spend.
Eleven people. Try filling a rotunda with eleven people. Ask again in April, I suppose.

lobby.name: Work the building
lobby.desc: Office to office, floor by floor. Coffee, one-pagers, favors remembered.
lobby.result: Four offices, two commitments, one 'send me the language.' The building runs on exactly this.

voices.text: Read the room right and four offices remember your name in March. That's the whole skill.
Charming doesn't skip a single deadline. Track which ones you spent today talking instead of filing.

start.text: Ground rules while it's quiet. Nothing in this building is owed to you — not a meeting, not a slot, not a microphone. Each week something happens, and the week is whatever that opens: a chair with fifteen minutes, a room worth packing, a door left ajar. When it opens, you get ONE real move — spend it or lose it. And what you spend your weeks doing, you get better at doing. Weeks disappear faster than you think. Lateral, crossover, conference, gone.

voices.text: No standing appointments. Openings only — and openings expire Friday. Finally, a calendar as honest as the real one.
Then read every room fast. The week that opens a door rarely announces which one.

choices.label: "Understood."
choices.reply: Sleep this week. You won't later.

w1-opening._note: Opening Day. The HR1 SNAP/Medicaid material that used to open this scene moved to its own week-3 event (w3-federal) 2026-08-15 — week 1 was doing two jobs and doing neither well. Keep this node about the room and the gap; the federal numbers belong to w3-federal, which is where their data lineage note now lives too.

start.text: Session opens today. Lei on every railing, the koa doors propped wide, somebody's grandmother already asleep in the gallery — and under all of it the arithmetic that will run this building until May. The Council on Revenues says $9.8 billion in general-fund taxes next year against a $10.6 billion budget. Everyone in the rotunda knows that number. Nobody has said out loud yet whose year it comes out of.

voices.text: Eight hundred million is not a rounding error and it is not a crisis either — it is a choice, and it gets made in about nine weeks.
Read the room today, not the spreadsheet. Half these people have already decided how this session goes and are waiting to see if you noticed.

choices.label: "We lead with who pays for it. Frame the gap as a choice, not weather."
choices.reply: The choice sets the terms. A gap is an accident; a choice has an author — and authors can be asked questions in public.

choices.label: "We lead with the math. Nothing moves unless it balances."
choices.reply: The money chairs will love this. The coalition will want to know the math includes people.

choices.label: Say nothing. Watch who talks to whom.
choices.reply: Two committee chairs and a lobbyist, in that order, in under a minute. The numbers do not improve under observation, but the room tells you things.

presser.text: Opening Day. Lei on every railing, three governors in the gallery — and the press set up on the makai steps, where your campaign has the 9 a.m. slot. One microphone, four minutes, every outlet in town. What's the message?

voices.text: Four minutes, every outlet in town. Read the room before you read the line.
Whatever you say, say it loud enough that the back row remembers it Monday.

choices.label: "Tax fairness, by name. The register pays more than the penthouse."
choices.reply: The crowd claps. Upstairs, two office doors close quietly. Grange, at the edge of the steps, writes one word on a legal pad.

choices.label: "Cost of living. Discipline. A budget that doesn't wobble."
choices.reply: Inside, the murmurs are approving. Somewhere on the sidewalk, a coalition text thread goes quiet.

choices.label: Four minutes of pure aloha — thank everyone, promise nothing.
choices.reply: Warm, safe, forgettable. Three offices call before lunch asking for 'whatever that one-pager was.'

unlocks._note: Opening Day opens the whole ground floor: the scripted week-1 talks (these used to live on the calendar entry) plus a first walk through the building.

carriers._note: The bills are already chosen when this plays (agenda lock -> runEvent), so this is the handoff, not a pitch. It exists to put two faces on the sentence 'members carry the bills' before the gauntlet starts.
carriers.text: Room 312, after the cameras leave. Two members are waiting for you, and between them they are the only reason your package exists as paper rather than opinion. Rep. X will file in the House this week and walk it through Finance. Sen. X gets it in April, if it lives that long, and has read exactly none of it yet. "So," Rep. X says, pulling the introduction forms over, "whose name goes first, and what do we do when Finance asks us to cut it?"

voices.text: Introduction is the one step that cannot fail. Everything after it can. Use the free step to set the terms.
Two members, two chambers, one package — and they have not talked to each other about it once. That is your job now, not theirs.

choices.label: "Both names on both bills. You two are a team before Finance is a problem."
choices.reply: Sen. X raises an eyebrow at being volunteered, then signs anyway. It costs you something upstairs — leadership notices members pairing off early — and buys you two people who now have to call each other.

choices.label: "Rep. X leads. Sen. X, stay clean until crossover."
choices.reply: A conventional, competent split. Rep. X takes the weight and the credit. Sen. X gets a package in April with somebody else's fingerprints on it, and remembers that.

choices.label: "We cut nothing. Tell Finance the number is the bill."

success.reply: Rep. X looks at the forms for a while. "If I say that in Finance, I own it — and if you leave me out there alone, I don't get it back." You tell them who is standing behind them, by name and by number. They file it whole.

failure.reply: "That's a great line for a rally," Rep. X says, not unkindly, "and I'm the one who has to say it to a chair who signs my committee assignments." The forms get filed. A trim is already implied.

start.speaker: kawaguchi
start.text: Kawaguchi doesn't look up from the committee referral sheet. "I schedule what can pass. The bills your people are carrying — I can hear one of them early, IF the ask is trimmed to something the floor survives. Or you keep the full number and wait for me to find a week. Maybe I find one."

voices.text: A trimmed bill that passes still moves real dollars. A poster that dies in committee moves none. Run the math before the ego does.
Trim it and the base watches you fold on the ask before the fight even starts. That costs more than $25M.
He said 'find a week.' Weeks are HIS. But a chair who names a date in front of a witness has spent something he can't unspend.

choices.label: Trim the ask. Get the early hearing.
choices.reply: "Smart." He initials the sheet. Your bill just got $25M/yr lighter — and a hearing date.

choices.label: Hold the number. "Find the week, chair."
choices.reply: A long pause. "Bold." It is not clear that 'bold' is a compliment on this floor.

choices.label: "Name the date, chair. In front of your team."

success.reply: He looks around the room, then at you, and writes a date on the referral sheet in pen. "February 14th. Don't make me regret the ink."

failure.reply: "In front of staff?" The sheet goes face-down. "I'll find a week." He will not find a week.

start.speaker: grange
start.text: Grange finds you by the koa doors, all smiles. "Big session, yeah? Our members can live with a lot — but the conveyance thing reads like a tax on selling your own house. Help me help you: carve out everything under three million, we stay neutral. Testify friendly, even."

voices.text: The bill already exempts owner-occupied homes under the standard threshold — that's not spin, that's the bill text. Cite it and watch him improvise.
Neutral-to-friendly from the roundtable is a real asset. Just don't pay for it with language the base will notice missing.

choices.label: "It already exempts owner-occupied homes. Read the bill, Curtis."
choices.reply: The smile holds, one degree cooler. "Then our testimony will read the bill very... closely."

choices.label: "Send me your carve-out language. No promises."
choices.reply: "That's all I ask." It is never all he asks.

choices.label: "Say it at the hearing, then. On the record, under your own name."

success.reply: The smile finally goes. "We don't usually testify on the record this early." They don't testify at all. Your bill gets a hearing without a villain in the room.

failure.reply: "Happy to!" And he does — warmly, at length, in favor of a version of your bill that does not exist. The committee writes down HIS number.

start.text: Rumor from the tax department: the Council on Revenues may shave the forecast at its next meeting. If it's true, every bill with a price tag gets harder. The coalition wants to know the campaign's posture before the papers ask.

voices.text: A rumor isn't a motion. Nothing on the floor changes until the Council actually meets and votes the number.
The building is already reading your posture. Silence is a message too — make sure it's the one you mean.
'May shave the forecast' is not a number. Somewhere there is a worksheet with a number on it. Ask for the worksheet.

choices.label: Go public first: "This is exactly why we fix revenue."
choices.reply: You beat the rumor to the microphone. The clip travels. So does your name, attached to the word 'taxes.'

choices.label: Brief the steering committee quietly. Keep powder dry.
choices.reply: Doors close, voices lower. The building notices a campaign that can keep its own counsel.

choices.label: Say nothing yet. Ask the department for the actual worksheet.

success.reply: Three pages of tables. The shave is 0.4 percent, not the two the rumor grew on the way over. You walk into the steering meeting with the real number and watch the room recalibrate around you.

failure.reply: You quote a line from the wrong column at the wrong meeting. It is corrected, gently, by someone junior to you.

start.text: Health department's in the hallway with a real one: a federal reimbursement fell through and a rural clinic network needs a $40M emergency appropriation to stay open through the fiscal year. The rescue coalition wants your campaign's name on the joint letter by Friday.

voices.text: Forty million to keep the doors open in places with one doctor per island district. The network that shows up for you in March is built on days like this.
Every emergency signed off-cycle is a line item nobody voted on in the open. Ask where the forty comes FROM before you sign.

choices.label: Sign the letter. Clinics stay open.
choices.reply: Your campaign's name goes second on the list. The clinic director cries in the hallway. The fiscal note does not.

choices.label: Ask for a scrubbed budget first. Defer.
choices.reply: Prudent, defensible — and the neighbor-island papers run 'LAWMAKERS STALL CLINIC RESCUE' anyway.

ev-emergency._atNote: `at` (map job B): the week-beat camera flies here before the event opens — rural clinic network, so the beat crosses to Hawaiʻi island. Spec: {island} frames the island; {island, px:[x,y]} targets a point in that island's BAKE pixels (anchor+scale transform, same as landmarks — never world px directly); absent = the Capitol. Most events correctly stay at the Capitol — the campaign happens there; give an event an address only when its scene genuinely is somewhere else.

start.text: Morning paper, page A1 turn: an op-ed titled 'The Last Tax Hike Hawaiʻi Can Afford,' signed by three retired executives. It names your bills. It is, annoyingly, well written.

voices.text: A well-written op-ed still gets the causation backwards. That's a teachable moment, if you can resist just yelling 'wrong.'
Three retired executives against school meals is a sentence that reads itself out loud. Consider letting it.

choices.label: Write the response yourself. Name the stakes, name the kids.
choices.reply: Your reply runs Sunday. The coalition shares it 400 times. One executive writes again; nobody reads the sequel.

choices.label: Let it breathe. Op-eds don't vote.
choices.reply: By Thursday it's fish wrap. The building respects a campaign that doesn't chase every ball.

choices.label: Skip the reply. Take it to live radio, unedited.

success.reply: Forty minutes, no filter, one host who lets you finish a sentence. By noon two of the three executives are being asked about THEIR taxes.

failure.reply: You are asked, four times, whether this is a tax increase. Four times you explain that it is complicated. The clip that travels is the fourth time.

start.text: Hearing day. Forty testifiers are signed up — teachers, a school cook, two ranchers, a hotel housekeeper with her whole shift outside. Two minutes each. The chair is already checking his watch. Somebody has to go first.

voices.text: The cook feeds four hundred kids a day. Put the number in the room, not just the argument.
The ranchers flip a room faster than anyone expects — 'small business supports this' still moves skeptics.

choices.label: The school cook goes first.
choices.reply: Two minutes, no notes. The chair stops checking his watch. Twitter does the rest.

choices.label: The ranchers go first.
choices.reply: 'We're not anti-business — we ARE the business.' Two committee skeptics visibly recalibrate.

choices.label: Neither. Fill the room past the sign-up sheet and let him try to gavel it.
choices._ante: The ante (engine: a checked choice's own `effects` are paid on commit, win or lose). Packing a room past the sign-up sheet SPENDS the base — you are asking people to take an unpaid morning off before you know whether the chair will seat them. It is printed on the button with the odds.

success.reply: By 9:40 the overflow room is full and they open a second overflow room. The chair, on the record, extends testimony by ninety minutes. Nobody in that hallway forgets that they are the reason.

failure.reply: Twenty-two show. The overflow room stays dark and the chair caps testimony at forty minutes, politely. The housekeeper who took an unpaid morning off does not get called.

start.text: Friday coalition potluck, church hall two blocks makai of the Capitol. Someone brought squid lūʻau, someone brought Costco chicken bake, and somebody's cousin on Senate staff brought a rumor about conference chairs. Attendance is, technically, optional.

voices.text: Half the real deals of the decade get made over paper plates. Go. Bring something store-bought and humble.
Go — but work the room. The staff there know which bills are actually moving, three weeks before the papers do.

choices.label: Go. Eat. Listen twice as much as you talk.
choices.reply: You learn two referral rumors and one recipe. The week ends warmer than it started.

choices.label: Skip it. The inbox is a crime scene.
choices.reply: Productive, lonely. Monday, everyone else shares an inside joke about the chicken bake.

start.text: Sine die. Lei on the podiums again, and the building exhales all at once. Whatever you moved this session is moving; whatever you didn't is next January's problem. Interim starts tomorrow — that's when we count what it all did.

voices.text: Rest. Then back to the gap — it doesn't adjourn just because the building does.
Adequate. Nobody bankrupted the place, which around here counts as a triumph. Ask again in January whether it still does.

choices.label: Walk out through the rotunda one more time.
choices.reply: The Capitol is open to the sky in the middle — by design. Money in, money out, and the weather gets a vote too.

start.text: The whiteboard by the door hasn't changed: bills are alive until a deadline says otherwise. Lateral and crossover weeks are where they go to die quietly — spend the one action you get where a week actually turns.

voices.text: Deadlines don't care how busy the week was. Neither does the whiteboard.

choices.label: "Thanks. Back to it."
choices.reply: Someone's taped a fresh sticky note under the deadline column: DRINK WATER. SESSIONS ARE CARDIO.

start.speaker: kawaguchi
start.text: "Every advocate who makes it up these stairs thinks their bill is the one the ceiling bends for." He taps the referral sheet. "Bring me something the floor survives, and we'll talk about ceilings."

voices.text: The ceiling is a CHOICE. Someone typed it into a spreadsheet. Ask which one.
The man guards the referral sheet. You will need him more than he needs you.

choices.label: "Noted, chair."
choices.reply: He almost smiles. Almost.

start.speaker: grange
start.text: "Nothing personal, ever — that's the first rule of this hallway." He offers macadamia candy from a tin. "Our members just want predictability. Tax bills are weather. We sell umbrellas."

voices.text: Predictability IS worth money. He's the most honest person on this floor, in the way a price tag is honest.
Take the candy. Audit the metaphor. Weather doesn't hire three lobbyists per raindrop.

choices.label: Take the candy. Keep walking.
choices.reply: It's good candy. It is always good candy.

start.text: The coalition count on the wall: 61 orgs on the meals bill, 40 on the credit, 'it's complicated' scrawled next to anything with the word conveyance in it. One big turnout moment fits in a month — whoever asks early gets it.

voices.text: This is your actual caucus. The one that shows up in matching shirts.
Sixty-one organizations, one shared printer. Respect the logistics or lose the coalition to burnout.

choices.label: "Give us two weeks' notice, always."
choices.reply: Noted on the wall. Two weeks is apparently considered a luxury.

choices.label: "Forget the calendar. What does the coalition actually need?"

success.reply: The math on the wall stops for a second. Someone writes: SOMEBODY TO NOT DISAPPEAR IN APRIL. Under it, in smaller writing, three more things — none of them a rally.

failure.reply: Same answer as always: bodies at a hearing. You asked a real question in a hallway, which is where real questions go to be small talk.

start.speaker: rep-x
start.text: "Everyone thinks introducing a bill is the hard part." They gesture at a shelf of binders, none of them yours. "Forty-one measures have my name on them this session. Three of them I'd take a bad meeting for. Tell me again why yours is one of the three."

voices.text: Forty-one introductions, and a member's real currency is which ones they spend a chair's patience on. You are asking for that, not for a signature.
They want to know the people behind it are real. Give them a district and a name, not a coalition letterhead.

choices.label: Give them the district numbers. Their district.
choices.reply: They read it twice. "Eleven hundred households in my precincts alone?" It goes in the top folder, which is a smaller folder than it sounds.

choices.label: "Because you'll be the one who passed it."
choices.reply: "Flattery." A pause. "Effective flattery, but flattery."

start.speaker: sen-x
start.text: "I'll be honest with you — I have not read it." Sen. X says this without embarrassment, because it is week one and reading it now would be a waste of a good afternoon. "Send it when the House has finished doing whatever the House is going to do to it. I'll read the version that actually reaches me."

voices.text: Cold, but correct. The Senate reads the bill that crosses over, not the one that was filed — those are frequently different documents.
'I have not read it' is not a brush-off, it's a schedule. Ask what would make them read it early.

choices.label: "Then read the fiscal note. Four pages, and it won't change."
choices.reply: "Four pages I can do." They take it. Somewhere in the building that is a substantial commitment.

choices.label: "Fair. I'll see you in April."
choices.reply: "You will." It is not warmth, exactly, but it is not nothing — most advocates argue with that sentence and lose the afternoon.

ev-introducer._note: The introducer-relationship event. Reachable from week 4 on via genericEvents. Deliberately a squeeze rather than a favour: the member is carrying real risk and asking the player to absorb some of it, which is what rapport actually buys.

start.speaker: rep-x
start.text: They catch you before the elevator, holding a marked-up copy of your own bill. "Leadership's office called. Not about your bill — about me." A committee assignment, a district project, a favour owed; the specifics don't matter and they don't offer them. "They'd like to know if I'm carrying this all the way or just filing it. I have to give them an answer this week, and whatever I say, I have to live in this building afterward."

voices.text: This is the pressure that never appears in a journal entry. No vote, no record — just a member deciding how much of their own year to spend on you.
They came to you first. That is the whole tell. Somebody who had already folded would have sent an email on Friday.
If the answer is 'you're on your own,' you don't get a second one of these. Members talk to each other more than they talk to us.

choices.label: "Tell them you're carrying it. We'll put people in your district behind you."
choices.reply: They exhale. "Then I'll say yes." You have just promised turnout in a district you do not organize yet, which is a problem for a future week and a real one.

choices.label: "Say whatever keeps you safe. I'd rather have you in April."
choices.reply: "...Thank you." Nobody in this hallway says that to a member, and it costs the bill something this week — but they will still be picking up the phone in April, which is more than most advocates can say.

choices.label: "Ask them to put that request in writing."

success.reply: Rep. X actually laughs. "They will never do that." Which is the point, and they see it a beat later: a request nobody will write down is a request nobody can enforce. The call is not returned, and the bill keeps its number.

failure.reply: "That's how you talk to an agency, not to the people who set my committee." They put the marked-up copy back in their bag. "I'll handle it my way." You do not learn what their way was.

w3-federal._note: The federal safety-net cuts, moved out of w1-opening 2026-08-15 so the material has a scene of its own. Grounded in ~/HawaiiAppleseed/snap-medicaid-timeline (repo dtomkatsu/Hawaii-Appleseed-website, medicaidData/snapData arrays) — federal HR1 SNAP/Medicaid cuts, all already in effect by this session's Jan 2027 start. Figures: SNAP-Ed eliminated 2025-10-01 (-$2.5M/yr); ABAWD work-req age 18-54 -> 18-64 2026-10-01 hits 16,570 adults 55-64 + 10,303 households w/ teens 14-18; Medicaid narrower immigrant eligibility + 6-month (was 12) recert already dropped an est. 1,200-2,400 people. Refresh these if the timeline's data updates. NOTE the player's own bills have not been heard yet (h-fin deadline is week 5) — nothing here may imply a hearing on them.

start.text:
The joint briefing runs in a hearing room too small for it, which is how you can tell the department expected fewer people. What Congress did to the safety net in HR1 is no longer a forecast — every piece of it is already law and most of it is already running.

SNAP-Ed is gone: over $2.5 million a year the state used to spend on nutrition classes and farmers'-market programs, zeroed out in October 2025. Work requirements now reach ages 55 to 64 — 16,570 adults in Hawaiʻi who were exempt a year ago — plus 10,300 households with teenagers. On Medicaid, narrower eligibility and twice-yearly recertification have already dropped an estimated 1,200 to 2,400 people from the rolls, not because they stopped qualifying but because they missed a form.

None of it appears as a federal line item anymore. It appears here, in a state budget that is already $800 million short.

voices.text: Read the caseload numbers, not just the caseload story. 16,570 and 10,300 are Hawaiʻi's own — DHS ran them, not a national estimate.
Every family that lost coverage over a missed form, not a change in income, just learned exactly how fragile 'eligible' really is. That is an organizing conversation, not a caseload stat.
Nobody in this room disputes the numbers. What they don't have is a sentence that connects a missed recertification form to a tax bill. That sentence is the entire job.

choices.label: "Then our bills are the answer to this. Say it that way, every time."
choices.reply: You watch it land. By afternoon two other organizations have picked up the framing, and one of them is a group that has never testified on a tax bill in its life.

choices.label: "Get me the recertification data. How many were actually still eligible?"

success.reply: It takes three calls and a very patient analyst, but the answer comes back: the overwhelming majority of the people dropped were still eligible when they were dropped. That is not a caseload decline. That is a paperwork failure with a body count, and now you can say so with a citation.

failure.reply: What comes back is a summary table with the eligibility field aggregated away — technically responsive, practically useless. You can say 'many were still eligible.' You cannot say how many, and in this building the difference between those two sentences is everything.

choices.label: Sit with it. Take the room's temperature before saying anything.
choices.reply: Three department staff, two providers and a health-center director, and not one of them says the word 'taxes.' They have been told not to. It is useful to know exactly who is not allowed to make your argument for you.

w4-souza._note: NO BANNER YET — the dialogue renders fine without an `art` key. Souza never appears on screen and has no talk slot: his scheduler, his committee members and a closed door speak for him, which is the whole argument of the week (moved from week 3 to week 4 on 2026-08-15 when w3-federal took week 3). The red check reads `yamamoto-open` (2026-08-19, user's call moved the Kawaguchi meeting to week 5 — its `souza-intro` flag no longer exists this early, so this now reads the co-chair's tip from w2-yamamoto instead): a player who spent Yamamoto's favor gets +3 here, and a player who never got in her office is rolling this cold. `souza-intro` still exists — it is set THREE WEEKS LATER, in w5-decking, and is spent in w8-crossover and w11-wam.

start.text: Money Committee Week. Ways and Means posts its notices Tuesday at four, and by twenty past, every advocate in the building has read them off a phone in the same hallway. You have called Souza's office six times. His scheduler is unfailingly warm, remembers your name without being told, and has nothing — not this week, not next, and the week after that is holding for the chair. Room 211 is the same koa as every other door on the floor. It is closed.

voices.text: Ways and Means is the last gate before conference and its deadline is week eleven. You have time. What you don't have is a way in.
Six calls and she still says your name warmly. That's a scheduler protecting a chair, not one brushing off a stranger — and the difference is worth something.
There are twelve other members on that committee, and not one of them has a scheduler holding weeks. A chair is not the only person in a room.

choices.label: Take whatever she offers. Any slot, any hour.
choices.reply: 7:40 on a Friday morning, three weeks out, fifteen minutes, subject to the chair's floor schedule. You take it and you write it in pen.

choices.label: Stop chasing the chair. Work the other twelve members.
choices.reply: Four offices in a day, two of them freshmen nobody has ever asked for anything. Thursday, a WAM member you have never met asks a question in a hearing that came straight off your one-pager.

choices.label: Catch him in the hallway when the notices post.

success.reply: Ninety seconds between the elevator and the stairwell, and he never once stops walking. But he answers. "Your problem isn't me. Your problem is the House sends me things in April and expects a miracle in May." The elevator takes him. You write the whole thing down on the back of the notice, standing up.

failure.reply: He is polite, which is worse. "Talk to my office." He is talking to somebody else before the sentence is finished, and you are standing in a hallway holding a notice you had already read.

w5-decking._note: DEADLINE WEEK, and THE KAWAGUCHI MEETING (moved here from week 2 on 2026-08-19, user's call — week 2 now belongs to co-chair Yamamoto, w2-yamamoto). Finance's referral deadline is week 5 (chairs.json stages.h-fin), and the date Kawaguchi may have named via the week-1 optional talk (`talk-kawaguchi`) is February 14th — THIS week — so a player who earned `kawaguchi-date` is walking in already owed something. TWO-PART ART carries over unchanged from the original placement: the dialogue-level `art` (w2-finance, the Beretania breezeway) carries the approach, the `office` node overrides it with w2-finance-office; renderNode reads `n.art || dlg.art`. Sets `souza-intro`, spent in w8-crossover and w11-wam — both AFTER this week, so the causality holds now that the meeting sits at week 5 instead of week 2. w4-souza used to read `souza-intro` from here when this was week 2; since the meeting is now three weeks LATER than w4-souza, that scene reads `yamamoto-open` (set in w2-yamamoto) instead — keep it that way, or w4 is checking a flag that cannot exist yet.

start.text: Fifteen minutes, his scheduler said, and she said it twice. So you wait in the breezeway where the trades come through, watching the courtyard fill and empty and fill. The lateral file goes up at four — Finance's own notice, the one that decides who gets heard this year and who doesn't. Kawaguchi called you up here himself, which nobody in this hallway does for a courtesy.

voices.text: Read the room right: a chair who wants you to hear something from him instead of off a printout is either doing you a favor or bracing you for a loss. Both cost him time he doesn't have today.
Decking day, and he still found fifteen minutes for you. That is not nothing, on the one day of the year he has none to spare.

choices.label: Bring the fiscal note. Fifteen minutes, one number.
choices.reply: You leave the binder in the bag and walk in with a single page.

choices.label: Bring the caseload pages. Fifteen minutes, one family.
choices.reply: Sixteen thousand five hundred and seventy adults, and one of them with a name and a district.

choices.label: Bring nothing. Let him say the first thing.
choices.reply: You go up empty-handed, which in this building is either confidence or a mistake, and nobody can tell which until afterward.

office.speaker: kawaguchi
office.text: He doesn't stand. "Sit. The notice goes up at four, and I wanted you to hear where you stand from me, not off a phone in that hallway with everyone else." He turns his chair a few degrees toward the window. "Eight hundred and seventy-six measures came to Finance last session. I heard a fraction of them and I'm not apologizing for the fraction." A pause, and this is the part he actually called you up here for. "My problem, if you make my notice, is that whatever I hear, Ways and Means hears after me. And Chris Souza hasn't returned a call of mine since November."

voices.text: 876 referrals, and this committee hands back one of the two lowest hearing rates in the building. He isn't being dramatic, he's quoting his own workload.
He just drew you the route: Finance, then Ways and Means. A bill he hears today is still a bill Souza can bury in April. Plan for two gates, not one.
"Hasn't returned a call since November" isn't a complaint, it's an offer. He wants something carried to the Senate that he can't be seen carrying himself.

choices.label: "Then tell me what Ways and Means needs to hear."
choices.reply: He writes two words on a legal pad, tears the sheet off and slides it across: FLOOR, NOT CEILING. "Souza doesn't care what your bill raises. He cares what it costs him in a bad year. Go answer that, and don't tell him I said so."

choices.label: "Hear one of ours early, chair. I'll fill your room."
choices.reply: "Everybody fills my room." But he writes something down, which is more than he did in January.

choices.label: "Call him. From this office, while I'm sitting here."

success.reply: He looks at you a long moment, then picks up the desk phone. He does not get Souza. He gets a scheduler — and he uses the chair's voice on her, the one he has not once used on you. "Jon Kawaguchi. Put them on the calendar." He hangs up. "That is the entire favor. Don't spend it saying hello."

failure.reply: "In my own office?" He puts one hand flat on the desk, which is as close as this man comes to raising his voice. "When I want the Senate to know what I'm doing, I'll tell them myself."

friday.text: Four o'clock. You're back in the hallway outside Finance with everyone else who doesn't have a chair's ear, watching the same door you just walked out of. Whatever he decided in there, the notice makes it official in twenty minutes — the same way it does for the forty other measures that got fifteen minutes and a closed door instead of an open one.

voices.text: Fifteen minutes with the chair is not a hearing. Whatever happens at four, you'll read it standing up, same as everyone who didn't get the meeting.

choices.label: Stay for the posting.
choices.reply: You stay. Whatever is on that notice, you will have watched it arrive — from a few feet closer than most people ever get.

w6-recess._note: THE MANDATORY RECESS. Const. art. III, sec. 10 requires a recess of at least five days somewhere between the 20th and 40th legislative day of every regular session; the dates themselves are set by concurrent resolution, not the constitution, and weekends, holidays and the recess days do not count toward the sixty. Anchored to real practice: the 2025 session opened Jan 15 and recessed Feb 20-26, which against sessionStart 2027-01-20 is exactly this week. NOT `noAction` — the CAPITOL is shut, the district is not, which is the entire scene. Grants rally/bench and deliberately withholds `push`: there is no chair in the building to work. The bite is mechanical, not textual: calendar `recess: true` makes resolveBills skip the week's chair rolls while every deadline stays where it was.

start.text:
The building empties on Thursday and does not fill again until the following Wednesday.

Nobody voted for this. The constitution requires it — at least five days of recess, somewhere between the twentieth and the fortieth legislative day — and the two chambers pick the actual dates between themselves by concurrent resolution. Sixty legislative days in a regular session. Five of them are gone by design, and the weekends and holidays around them were never counted in the sixty to begin with.

What that means for you is arithmetic, and it is not friendly. No notices post. No committee meets. No chair schedules anything. And not one deadline in front of you moves by a single day.

voices.text: Read it exactly: the recess suspends the WORK, not the clock. Every deadline you are running at is still where it was on Wednesday, with one fewer week to reach it.
Sixty legislative days to move a budget the size of a small country's. This is the week to notice how few that actually is.
Fifty-one members just went home to their districts. For five days the people who are hardest to reach in Honolulu are sitting in a folding chair at a community meeting on their own island.
Everyone you have been chasing is unreachable and so is everyone chasing you. That cuts both ways, and it will not happen again this session.

choices.label: Go home. Sleep. Be at the Saturday cleanup like a person.
choices.reply: You pull weeds at the stream cleanup for four hours beside people who have been getting your emails since January and had never once seen your face on a Saturday. Nobody talks about the bill. Everybody notices you came.

choices.label: District week: work the neighbor-island offices while members are home.

success.reply: Three islands in four days on the cheapest flights that exist. You catch a WAM member at her own district office with no scheduler between you, in slippers, at four in the afternoon — fifty minutes, no gatekeeper, and a question at the end that means she read it. Room 211 could not have bought you that.

failure.reply: Two locked doors, one staffer covering three offices, and a member who is genuinely, visibly on vacation with her grandchildren and does not want to be your Tuesday. You apologize and mean it. The flights were not cheap.

choices.label: Work the recess like it isn't one. Draft the Ways and Means amendment now.

success.reply: Five days, no phone, no hallway. You come back with the Senate draft finished and a fiscal note that answers the question Souza actually asks — not what it raises, what it costs him in a bad year. It is sitting in a drawer, ready, weeks before anyone will ask for it.

failure.reply: You spend five days alone with a document and produce eleven pages nobody asked for. On Wednesday the building comes back rested and you come back with a draft and a headache.

choices.label: Put the coalition on planes. Five days of rooms nobody is watching.
choices.reply: Four islands, eleven rooms, no press and no member in any of them. The organizing that shows up in April is built in weeks exactly like this one, which is why it is invisible in March.

back.text: Wednesday morning the doors open and the hallway is loud again, and everyone in it is one week closer to a deadline that did not move.

voices.text: Nothing was heard while you were gone. Nothing could be. The window you have left just got shorter by one, and the odds on every chair went up accordingly.

choices.label: Back to work.
choices.reply: Back to work.

w7-storm._note: PRE-EVENT: pinned to week 7 by calendar `pre`, so it runs BEFORE the week's own event and is tracked in S.preDone, not S.eventDone. A -600000 revenueK hit ($600M) lands on the SAME FY2027 scoreboard as everything else (PolicyPanel.external via syncScore) — it does not kill any bill, it re-prices the whole session by moving the number the campaign has to cover. Sized deliberately: it is roughly fifteen times ev-emergency's $40M clinic rescue and is meant to be the moment the player's revenue arithmetic stops being comfortable. The state share is the teaching point — a federal declaration reimburses most of a disaster and the state carries the rest, immediately, out of a budget that was already short.

start.text:
The Kona low sat over the chain for three days.

By the time it moved off, Kauaʻi had lost two highway bridges, Maui had six hundred homes with water through them, and the Kāneʻohe side of Oʻahu was a slow brown river with cars in it. Nobody died, which everyone keeps saying out loud, in the tone people use when they are not yet sure they believe it.

The Governor declares an emergency Sunday night. The federal declaration follows on Tuesday, which covers a large share of it eventually, on a reimbursement schedule measured in years. What it does not cover, and what cannot wait for years, is the state's own share: emergency housing, the two bridges, debris removal, the water systems on three islands, and the harbor.

Budget and Finance puts a working number on it Wednesday morning. Six hundred million dollars.

voices.text: Six hundred million against a budget that was already eight hundred million short. That is not a line item — it is the whole argument of your session, restated at gunpoint.
This will move as an emergency appropriation and it will move FAST, ahead of everything, because it has to. Every hour Finance spends on it is an hour not spent on your notice.
Six hundred families in shelters in Wailuku tonight. Whatever this does to the arithmetic, that is what the arithmetic is about.
Watch what happens to the phrase 'we can't afford it' this week. It is about to get very cheap, and it is about to get very expensive.

choices.label: Say the obvious thing: this is what revenue is FOR.
choices.reply: You say it Wednesday, in front of a camera, while the water is still in people's houses. Half the building thinks you are the only honest person in it and the other half thinks you just used a disaster as a talking point, and both halves say so.

choices.label: Say nothing this week. Send the coalition's vans to Wailuku.
choices.reply: Eleven vans, four days, no press release. On Friday a member you have never gotten a meeting with texts your organizer directly to ask where to send her church's donations.

choices.label: Get in front of the appropriation: draft the pay-for and hand it over.

success.reply: You are in Finance's anteroom Thursday at seven in the morning with three pages: what the state share actually is, what the rainy-day fund can carry without a downgrade, and what the gap is after both. It is the first document anyone has handed them that ends in a number instead of a request. The gap does not go away. But it is now YOUR framing of the gap that the committee is arguing inside of.

failure.reply: You are in the anteroom at seven with three pages nobody asked you for, on the one morning of the year when the Finance staff have a genuine emergency and a chair standing over them. The analyst takes it politely. You watch her put it face-down on a stack.

cost.text:
The emergency appropriation passes both chambers inside nine days, which is the fastest anything will move all session. Nobody votes against it. Nobody would.

And on Friday the FY2027 sheet is reissued with the state share in it, and everything you have been carrying since January is now being weighed against a number six hundred million dollars worse than the one you started from.

Nothing in your package changed. The floor under it did.

voices.text: Nine days, unanimous, no hearing worth the name. Money moves at exactly the speed the building agrees it has to — remember that the next time somebody tells you the process is why your bill is slow.
Your bills are all still alive and all still exactly where they were. What moved is the standard they will be judged against in conference.
This is the lesson nobody teaches in a civics class: a budget is not a document, it is a running argument, and the weather gets a vote.

choices.label: Take the number.
choices.reply: Six hundred million dollars, on your scoreboard, in a column you did not put it in. It is going to sit there for the rest of the session.

w8-crossover._note: DEADLINE WEEK: third reading in the originating chamber (chairs.json stages.h-floor, deadline 8). Crossover is the session's hardest wall and its most misunderstood one — a bill that crosses is not halfway home, it is starting over in a chamber that owes it nothing. Runs before the week's floor roll; never state the outcome. The 48-hour decking rule is real: a bill must be printed and on members' desks 48 hours before final reading.

start.text:
Crossover.

Everything the House is going to send the Senate this year has to pass third reading by Thursday, and everything it does not send is dead until January. The 48-hour rule means the bills had to be printed and on the desks by Tuesday, which means the real deadline was two days before the deadline, which is a sentence that has ended more campaigns than any vote ever taken.

The floor calendar runs to ninety-odd measures. They will move most of them in a day and a half, with the clerk reading numbers and members voting on titles they last read in committee, if then.

voices.text: The 48-hour decking rule is not a formality — it is why the fight is over before the vote. By the time anyone is voting, the argument is two days cold.
A member who votes yes on crossover is doing you a small favour and telling the other chamber it is now their problem. Do not mistake it for a commitment.
Whatever crosses, crosses at whatever size it came out of Finance. Nobody is going to make your bill bigger in the Senate. This is the ceiling.

choices.label: Whip the floor. Every office, both sides of the aisle, two days.
choices.reply: Forty-some doors. You get eleven real conversations, four of which are with members who were always yes and one of which is with somebody who tells you something true about a colleague and asks you never to say where you heard it.

choices.label: Fill the gallery. Let them vote with the room watching.
choices.reply: Two hundred people in a gallery built for ninety, in matching shirts, silent because the sergeant-at-arms asked them to be, which is somehow louder. It is on the news at six.

choices.label: Stop working the House. Start working the Senate NOW, before it crosses.

success.reply: It is the counterintuitive move and it is the right one: the bill's fate in the Senate is being decided this week by people who have not been asked about it yet. By Thursday two WAM offices have already read it — not because it crossed, but because you got there before it did.

failure.reply: You spend crossover week in the wrong building. The Senate offices are polite and unhurried and entirely uninterested in a measure that has not reached them, and behind you the House votes without you in the hallway.

after.text:
Thursday afternoon the clerk finishes reading, the gavel comes down, and every measure that made it walks across the rotunda to a chamber where nobody has ever heard of it, nobody sponsored it, and nobody owes it anything at all.

Half the session is behind you. The half in front of you starts from zero.

voices.text: New chamber, new committee, new chair, new deadlines. The record you built in the House is worth exactly what the Senate decides it is worth, which is usually nothing.
Your people just won something. Tell them. A campaign that only reports losses trains everyone to stop reading.

choices.label: Cross the rotunda.
choices.reply: You cross the rotunda.

w11-wam._note: DEADLINE WEEK: Ways and Means referral deadline (chairs.json stages.s-wam, deadline 11) — the last committee gate before conference. This is the PAYOFF of w4-souza's closed door and reads its flags: `souza-intro` (Kawaguchi's phone call, set in w5-decking) and `recess-draft` (the recess spent drafting the Senate amendment). Souza still never appears on screen — his scheduler, his committee and a closed door speak for him, exactly as in w4.

start.text:
Ways and Means decks Friday, and after Ways and Means there is no more committee. Whatever is on that notice goes to conference. Whatever is not is finished, in a chamber that never held a hearing on it, having crossed the rotunda for nothing.

Room 211 is the same closed koa door it was in February. But the anteroom is different now: there are eleven people in it and every one of them is carrying a measure that already passed the other chamber. This is the bottleneck the whole building funnels into, and it is one man's calendar.

voices.text: Last gate. After this the only thing left is conference, and conference does not add bills — it only cuts the ones already in it.
876 referrals to Finance, 936 to Ways and Means. He is the busiest gate in the building and he is the last one. Both facts are working against you at once.
Eleven people in an anteroom, all of whom got further than most. Being here is not an achievement any more. It is a queue.

choices.label: Spend the whole relationship. Everything you have built, now.

mods.label: the amendment you drafted in recess

success.reply: Twenty minutes, and not with him — with his analyst and his vice-chair, in a room with the door open, which is how you can tell it is real. They do not promise you the notice. They ask you three questions about the fiscal note, and the third one is a question you can only ask about a bill you are planning to post.

failure.reply: You get the scheduler, who is warm and remembers your name and has nothing, exactly as she had nothing in February. Nine months of work and the same sentence. You do not get to be angry at her; she is the only person in this building who has never once lied to you.

choices.label: Forget the chair. Twelve other members sit on that committee.
choices.reply: Four offices in a day and two of them freshmen nobody has asked for anything all session. On Wednesday a WAM member asks a question in a hearing that came straight out of your one-pager, and the chair looks up.

choices.label: Go public. Name the committee, name the number, name the week.
choices.reply: It runs Thursday: the bill, the deadline, the room number and the six hundred million reasons the state suddenly needs the money. Your coalition has never been louder. Room 211 has never been more closed.

twelve.text:
Friday at four the Ways and Means notice posts, the same way Finance's did in February, to the same hallway full of the same people.

This is the last one of these. After Friday there is nothing left to be posted to.

voices.text: Count what is left: conference in week fifteen, final reading in week sixteen. Two beats. Everything still alive after tonight is in the endgame.

choices.label: Wait for four o'clock.
choices.reply: You wait for four o'clock.

w13-crossover2._note: DEADLINE WEEK: second crossover, third reading in the second chamber (chairs.json stages.s-floor, deadline 13). Teaching point is CARRYOVER: Hawaii runs a two-year biennium, so a bill that dies in the first year is not gone — it sits in the chamber it died in and can be revived in the second. That is both a genuine consolation and the most effective way ever invented to make an advocate accept a loss quietly, and the scene should let both readings stand.

start.text:
Second crossover, and it is the quiet one. No gallery, no cameras, no matching shirts — everybody spent those in March. The Senate reads the House measures on third reading, the House reads the Senate's, and by Thursday the year's legislation is a fixed list that nothing can be added to.

What survives goes to conference. What does not is dead for the year, and 'for the year' is doing a lot of work in that sentence.

voices.text: Carryover: this is the first year of a two-year biennium, so a measure that dies now stays alive on the file and can be taken up again next January. It does not have to be reintroduced.
Be careful how you sell carryover to people who took a day off work to testify in February. 'We'll get it next year' is true and it is also the most effective sedative in this building.
Next January the revenue picture will be the storm plus a year of recovery. A bill that carries over does not carry over into the same budget it was written for.

choices.label: Tell the coalition the truth about carryover, all of it.
choices.reply: You say it plainly on the Thursday call: what carries over, what that is actually worth, and why next year is a different budget. Nobody thanks you for it. Two organizers who were about to quit do not quit.

choices.label: Say nothing yet. Everything alive needs you in conference, not on a call.
choices.reply: The call gets postponed to next week and then to the week after. You are not wrong about where the work is. The people who filled a hearing room in February find out from a newsletter.

choices.label: Work the floor one more time for whatever is still on the bubble.

success.reply: Forty-eight hours, no notice, and you put enough real constituents on enough real phones that two members who were going to be conveniently absent for third reading are in their chairs when the clerk reads the number.

failure.reply: You have asked these people for something in eleven of the last thirteen weeks. The list is tired. You get a fraction of what the same ask got you in February, and the fraction is the news.

list.text:
Thursday evening the list closes. Whatever is on it is the year.

Conference convenes next week, behind doors, with no public testimony and no more amendments from the floor. From here on, everything that happens to your bills happens in a room you cannot enter, decided by people whose names get posted on Monday.

voices.text: No testimony in conference. No public hearing on the final draft. The most consequential week of the session is the least visible one, and that is not an accident.

choices.label: Wait for Monday's list of conferees.
choices.reply: You wait for Monday.

w15-crunch._note: DEADLINE WEEK: conference (chairs.json stages.conf, deadline 15). The conference roll in resolveBills is AUTOMATIC and halves a bill on a miss — the highest-stakes check in the game and the only one the player never opts into — so this scene exists to make the player feel it coming rather than discover it in a status word. Grange returns here because conference is where the business roundtable's access is worth the most and the coalition's is worth the least.

start.text:
Conference. Room 309, and you are not in it.

Six people — three from each chamber, named Monday — sitting at a table with the House draft on one side and the Senate draft on the other, and a deadline Friday. There is no public testimony. There is no hearing. There is a clock and a stack, and at some point after ten at night somebody says a number and somebody else says a smaller number.

Grange has been in that hallway since Tuesday morning. He is not in the room either. He does not have to be; he has been in it for thirty years.

voices.text: Conference cannot add anything. It can only cut, merge, or let something die by running out the clock — and running out the clock is what it does most.
Everything gets decided against one figure now, and that figure has six hundred million dollars of storm in it. Your number is not competing with zero. It is competing with a bridge on Kauaʻi.
The conferees are named. That is the entire public record you get. Every other thing you learn this week, you learn from somebody who should not have told you.
This is the week the campaign either has durability or does not, and there is nothing left to do about which. Whatever you built by now is what walks into that room with your bill.

choices.label: Hold the number. No deal that cuts it, and say so out loud.
choices.reply: You tell all six conferees, in writing, that the coalition will not support a diluted version. It is a real position honestly held and it is also a gun pointed at your own foot, and every person you hand it to understands both halves.

choices.label: Take the deal. Something at sixty percent beats nothing at a hundred.
choices.reply: You let it be known, quietly, that you can live with a smaller number. It is in front of the conferees within the hour, which tells you exactly how closely somebody was listening for it.

choices.label: Find Grange in the hallway and ask him what he is actually protecting.

success.reply: He tells you, because at this hour of this week it costs him nothing and he has always slightly enjoyed you. It is not your bill. It is one clause in it, worth a fraction of the total, and he has been spending a week of a thirty-year reputation on it. You have been defending the whole thing against a man who only ever wanted one paragraph.

failure.reply: "Long week," he says, and means it, and asks after your family, and means that too, and tells you nothing at all. He is very good at this. It is genuinely a pleasure to watch, right up until you are back in the hallway with what you came with.

friday.text:
Friday. The conference deadline is tonight, and everything not agreed by midnight dies where it sits — no vote, no record, the same death as February, at the other end of the session.

You will find out in the morning. Everyone will.

voices.text: One more beat after this: final reading, week sixteen. Nothing agreed tonight can be changed then. Whatever comes out of 309 is the bill.

choices.label: Wait it out in the hallway.
choices.reply: You wait it out in the hallway, with everyone else who cannot go in.

w2-yamamoto._note: Week 2's courtesy call — now with the co-chair, not the chair (2026-08-19, user's call: "week 5 will be the meeting with Kawaguchi... week 2 will be the meeting with the co-chair of House Finance, Jennifer Yamamoto"). New character (characters.yamamoto), no card/portrait — same precedent as Grange and Souza, fully negotiated but no banner art yet. Sets `yamamoto-open`, which w4-souza reads in place of the `souza-intro` bonus that used to be set here — that flag moved to week 5 with Kawaguchi (w5-decking) and cannot exist this early any more. THE PLAYER'S BILLS ARE NOT HEARD YET — Finance's referral deadline is still week 5 (chairs.json stages.h-fin) — so nothing here may imply a hearing has happened or been scheduled.

start.text: Her door is already open when you get there, which after two weeks of scheduled fifteen-minute slots feels almost suspicious. "Jon doesn't do the meet-and-greet circuit," she says, not looking up from a stack of referral folders three feet high. "Somebody on Finance should. Sit — tell me what you actually need, not the one-pager version."

voices.text: Co-chairs carry the workload the chair doesn't have time for. She reads more bills than he does; she just doesn't get to keep any of them.
She can't schedule a hearing — that pen is his, not hers. What she CAN do is tell you things before he decides anything.

choices.label: Give her the real number, not the press version.
choices.reply: She writes it down on the folder itself, not a legal pad — in this building, that is the difference between a note and a record.

choices.label: Tell her about the family behind the caseload, not the fiscal note.
choices.reply: She listens the whole way through without once glancing at the folders. "That's the version he needs. He won't ask for it himself."

choices.label: Ask her the question everyone's afraid to: what actually gets a bill heard here?
choices.reply: She almost laughs. "Nobody's asked me that directly in six years." Whatever she tells you next, she's telling you because you asked instead of pitched.

office.speaker: yamamoto
office.text: She finally looks up. "Before this, I was a committee analyst — six years, Ways and Means, Senate side. I wrote the fiscal notes Souza's office actually reads." She taps the folder stack. "Jon schedules. I read. Between the two of us we see everything that comes through this room, and half of what happens in the other one." A pause. "You'll want something from over there eventually. Everybody does. I still owe a few people phone calls I never made."

voices.text: A former WAM analyst reading your fiscal note is not the same as a stranger reading it. She will know exactly which number is soft before you do.
"Owes some people phone calls" is an offer with the ask left off. Don't make her spell out the rest in front of anyone.
She hands you her own history inside of ten minutes. That is either instinct or a test, and it doesn't much matter which — you answer it the same way.

choices.label: "What should the fiscal note actually say?"
choices.reply: She pulls a pen and marks up your draft live, the way she must have marked up hundreds for a chair who never once said thank you. "This clears their staff review. Whether it clears Souza is a different problem — that one isn't mine to solve."

choices.label: "Put in a word for us over there, if you still can."

success.reply: She makes one call, off the record, to a Ways and Means clerk who still owes her a favor from 2019. "It's not an introduction," she says after she hangs up. "It's a name that won't get your call screened. That's all six years buys you now."

failure.reply: "I'm a House member now," she says, not unkindly, closing the folder. "That door isn't mine to open twice in one career, and it's not open today."

choices.label: "Just tell me what Kawaguchi actually wants to hear."
choices.reply: "Ask him," she says, and for the first time all meeting, offers nothing else. Some doors, even she only opens one at a time.

start.speaker: yamamoto
start.text: "Everybody wants Jon's pen. Nobody wants my folders." She taps the stack anyway. "The folder is where a bill actually lives, before it's a headline."

voices.text: The folder is the fiscal note, the referral history, every amendment offered and withdrawn. The headline is none of that.
She is telling you, gently, to read the paperwork before you ask anyone for a miracle.

choices.label: "Noted, co-chair."
choices.reply: She almost smiles — the same economical almost her chair uses. Maybe it's a Finance thing.

skillStart._ranksNote: Plain-language name for each skill level, INDEXED BY THE VALUE — ranks[1] is what a 1 is called, ranks[3] what a 3 is called. Re-based 2026-08-15 (user's call) so 1 = Very weak and 3 = Average: the ladder runs to 6, so the midpoint, not the floor, is what 'average' should name — everyone STARTS very weak and buys their way up. The list must cover 0 through `cap` or a level renders unnamed; index 0 exists only defensively (base is 1, and the creation screen's minus button floors at base, so nothing should ever reach it).

_unlocksNote: Talk story and actions are NOT a weekly allowance (changed 2026-08-15). Each event dialogue carries `unlocks` = {talks: {charId: dialogueId}, actions: [actionId]} applied when the event completes; a choice's effects may also carry `unlock` (same shape) for outcome-dependent doors. Action id 'push' opens the work-the-chair rows. A week whose event grants nothing is a closed building — renderHub says so explicitly. talkDefaults was removed with this change; the old week-1 calendar `talks` moved into w1-opening.unlocks. Keep every generic event granting SOMETHING or its week is dead air, and check the rotation after pinning a scripted week (see CLAUDE.md).
_calendarNote: Week 6 is the MANDATORY RECESS (Const. art. III, sec. 10: at least five days, somewhere between the 20th and 40th legislative day, with the actual dates fixed by concurrent resolution rather than the constitution). It carries `recess: true`, which makes resolveBills SKIP the chair rolls for that week WITHOUT moving any deadline — the whole lesson. Do not give it `noAction`: the Capitol is shut, the district is not, so w6-recess grants rally/bench and withholds `push`. Week 7 carries `milestone: false` so it can hold the storm `pre` without claiming a tick on a 940px strip already carrying twelve. `pre` runs BEFORE the week's own event and is tracked separately in S.preDone.
_yamamotoNote: Added 2026-08-19 (user's call: the week 2 meeting belongs to the co-chair, not the chair — Kawaguchi's own meeting moves to week 5, decking day). No `card` — same as Grange and Souza, a fully-negotiated character who simply has no banner photo yet; add one later per BANNERS.md's recipe if that changes. Her only mechanical output is the `yamamoto-open` flag (w2-yamamoto), which w4-souza now reads in place of the old `souza-intro` bonus — that flag moved to week 5 with Kawaguchi and can no longer be set early enough for week 4.
